title: The Phone-Free Weekend

lines.text: Today we're talking about a challenge I took last month: a whole weekend without my phone.
Nadia, I can't imagine that. What did your friends say when you told them?
They said I would be back online by lunchtime. My brother even bet me a pizza.
And did you lose the bet?
No. I told him on Sunday evening that I hadn't touched it once, and he had to pay.
What was the hardest part?
The first morning. I kept reaching for my pocket, although the phone was in a drawer.
Did you feel anxious?
At first, yes. Then I noticed that I was reading a real book for the first time in months.
I've read that people who check their phones less sleep better. Did you find that?
I did, actually. I slept for nine hours on Saturday, which almost never happens.
Would you do it again?
Probably, but not every weekend. I'd keep it for emergencies, and my boss said she would call only if something was really urgent.

title: Waiting for the Snow Leopard
focus: Narrative tenses (past simple, past continuous, past perfect)

lines.text: Kit, your photo of a snow leopard won a prize. How long did it take?
Nearly three weeks in the mountains. By the time I took it, I had been sitting in the same spot for eleven days.
Eleven days? What were you doing all that time?
Mostly waiting. I was wearing three jackets, and my hands had gone numb.
Did you ever think about giving up?
Every single night. On the tenth day I'd almost decided to go home when a local guide pointed at a ridge.
And the leopard was there?
Not yet. We were watching the ridge when the wind changed, and then she simply walked into view.
What went through your mind?
Honestly, nothing. I had been so tired that I almost missed it, but my hands knew what to do.
Would you say patience matters more than equipment?
In my job, yes. A good camera is useful, but the animals decide when the picture happens.

title: Planning the Book Sale
focus: Suggestions and possibility (could, might, how about, why don't we)

lines.text: Right, let's start. The book sale is in three weeks, and we still haven't decided where to hold it.
We could use the main hall, but the floor will be damaged if we put heavy tables on it.
What about the playground? It might rain, of course, but we could put up a tent.
A tent would cost money. How about asking the sports club to lend us theirs?
I'm fairly sure they'd say yes. They owe us a favour after last year.
Good. And who's going to collect the donated books?
I suggest that Dev and I do it on Saturday morning. We'll need a van.
My cousin has one. He might be willing to drive it, as long as we pay for the petrol.
That seems reasonable. Shall we fix the prices now?
Why don't we keep it simple? Everything is one pound, except large books, which are two.
Fine, but I'd suggest a free table for children's books. It would bring in families.
Great idea. I'll make the posters this week.
Perfect. Let's meet again next Tuesday to check progress.

title: Staying Safe in a Heatwave
focus: Conditionals with unless, as long as and in case

lines.text: With temperatures expected to stay high all week, we asked Dr Wilson how to stay safe.
The key advice is to drink water regularly, even if you don't feel thirsty.
Many people drink coffee instead. Is that a problem?
In moderation, no. But unless you also drink water, you can become dehydrated quickly.
What about going outside?
Avoid the hottest hours, roughly between noon and four in the afternoon, unless you really have to go out.
What should people wear?
Light, loose clothes and a hat. Dark colours absorb more heat, so choose pale ones.
Are some people at greater risk?
Yes. Older people and small children, in particular. Check on your neighbours, in case they need help.
And if someone feels dizzy?
Move them to a cool place and give them water. If they don't improve within half an hour, call a doctor.
Thank you, Dr Wilson. Stay cool, everyone.

title: Social Media and Teenagers
focus: Obligation, prohibition and permission (should, must, ought to, be allowed to)

lines.text: Tonight's question: should there be a minimum age for social media? Amara, you first.
Yes. Younger teenagers shouldn't be allowed to use platforms designed to keep them scrolling for hours.
I disagree with a total ban. Teenagers ought to learn to use these tools, and parents must guide them, not forbid them.
But not every parent has the time to supervise. Companies have a duty to protect young users.
I agree they should be more responsible. For example, they could be required to switch off notifications at night.
Liam, isn't a ban simpler?
Simpler, yes, but easy to get around. Many children simply lie about their age.
That's a weak argument. We don't abandon rules about alcohol just because some people break them.
Fair, but alcohol isn't a way of staying in touch with friends. Isolation is a real risk too.
Then perhaps we need a middle path: access with limits, not a complete ban.
I could accept that, as long as the limits are decided with young people, not just for them.
It sounds like you're closer than you thought. Thank you both.

title: Colour and Shopping
focus: Hedging language (tend to, may, seem, apparently)

lines.text: Today's topic is colour and shopping. Companies spend a great deal of money choosing colours, and it's not by accident.
Let's start with red. It tends to attract attention, which is why it appears on sale signs in so many shops.
However, we should be careful. Research on colour often produces mixed results, and cultures differ.
In some countries, white is linked with weddings, while in others it is associated with mourning.
Blue, on the other hand, seems to suggest trust, so banks and technology firms often choose it.
Many fast food chains use red and yellow. It may be that these colours encourage quick decisions, although the evidence is not conclusive.
What does appear fairly clear is that packaging matters. People often judge a product before they have tried it.
So the colour of a box may influence the price a customer expects to pay.
Should we conclude that colour controls us? Certainly not. It seems to nudge us, nothing more.
For your assignment, choose a local brand and analyse its colours. Say what you think they're meant to communicate.
And remember to use cautious language. Phrases like it seems and it may be are perfectly acceptable in academic writing.
That's all for today. See you on Thursday.

title: The Party That Nearly Wasn't
focus: Past perfect; would as future in the past

lines.text: Jorge, how was Marta's surprise party? I heard something went wrong.
Oh, it was chaos. We had planned everything for weeks, but by seven o'clock nobody had arrived.
Nobody? Why not?
I'd sent the invitations to the wrong address. Half the guests had gone to Marta's old flat.
Oh no. What did you do?
I called them, and they said they'd come straight away. Meanwhile, Marta was already walking up the street.
Did she see the decorations?
Not yet. I'd hidden the balloons in the bathroom, so the room looked empty. I thought she would be disappointed.
So what happened?
She walked in, saw me alone with a cake, and burst out laughing. She'd assumed we had forgotten her birthday.
And the guests?
They arrived ten minutes later, shouting surprise at the wrong moment. It was the best party we'd ever had.
Sounds like a perfect disaster.
It was. Next year, though, I'll check the address twice.

title: Working Alone, Together
focus: Gerunds as subjects and after prepositions

lines.text: Welcome to The Daily Shift. I'm Sam, and with me is Aiden, who has worked from home for four years.
Thanks, Sam. Working from home is brilliant in many ways, but it isn't perfect.
What do you miss most?
Chatting with colleagues over coffee. Being alone all day can make you feel strangely disconnected.
How do you deal with that?
I've started going to a shared office twice a week. Meeting other freelancers has made a big difference.
Some people complain about wasting time on video calls. Do you agree?
Partly. Having too many meetings is the problem, not the technology. I'm good at avoiding the unnecessary ones now.
Any advice for someone new to remote work?
Set a routine. Getting dressed properly, even if nobody sees you, helps you switch into work mode.
And finishing on time?
That's the hardest. Closing the laptop at five feels impossible when the office is also your living room.
So, in short, it's a matter of balancing freedom and structure.
Exactly. Thanks for having me.

title: Where Is My Suitcase?

lines.text: Good evening. How can I help you?
Hello. I'd like to report a missing suitcase. I arrived on the flight from Madrid, but my bag never came out.
I'm sorry to hear that. Could you tell me what it looks like?
It's a large green suitcase with a yellow ribbon on the handle.
Do you know whether there was a name tag on it?
Yes, my name and phone number were on it. Do you think you could check where it is?
Certainly. I'll look it up. Would you mind waiting a moment?
Not at all.
It seems it was left at the previous airport. It should arrive on tomorrow's first flight.
Tomorrow? I have a business presentation at nine, and my clothes are in that bag.
I understand. I can't promise anything, but I could arrange for it to be delivered to your hotel by noon.
Could you also tell me whether the airline pays for essentials in the meantime?
Yes, up to a limit. Keep your receipts, and we'll refund you.
That's helpful. Thank you for your patience.
